intervention_or_method.quote: we propose ISO-RAG (ISOperimetric Retrieval-Augmented Generation), a geometry-aware local graph retrieval framework for multi-hop QA.

results.quote: Evaluated with Qwen-Plus, the framework peaks at an F1 score of 42.8, securing an approximate 25% relative gain over HippoRAG2.
QA evaluation using Qwen3-Max yields an F1 score of 84.7 and an EM score of 80.7.
ISO-RAG achieves peak results by pruning only 32%. This proves multi-hop retrieval requires topology-aware filtering, not indiscriminate pruning.

main_finding.value: ISO-RAG reduces hallucinations and improves factual accuracy, coherence, and relevance of generated responses compared to existing methods.
main_finding.quote: These results confirm the efficacy of ISO-RAG in structured multi-hop scenarios, where preserving valid intermediate hops and suppressing spurious diffusion are critical.

study_design.quote: A 2-period crossover design was used: 2 pharmacists independently reviewed 213 outpatient prescriptions under both unaided and AI-assisted conditions, yielding paired unaided and collaborative results for each prescription.

population_or_dataset.quote: 2 pharmacists independently reviewed 213 outpatient prescriptions under both unaided and AI-assisted conditions, yielding paired unaided and collaborative results for each prescription.

intervention_or_method.quote: A structured knowledge base derived from drug package inserts served as the principal reference and supported lightweight knowledge augmentation through exact-match injection.

comparator.value: Unaided pharmacist review and stand-alone AI review
comparator.quote: Plain AI review and knowledge-augmented AI review were also run on the same 213-prescription test set to quantify hallucination rates, and stand-alone AI performance was assessed against the reference standard.

results.quote: Knowledge augmentation reduced the model hallucination rate from 19.7% (42/213 prescriptions) to 4.7% (10/213), an absolute reduction of 15.0 percentage points (relative reduction 76.2%; P<.001).
Overall review accuracy was 97.2% (207/213, 95% CI 94.0%-98.7%) in the human-AI collaborative condition vs 82.6% (176/213, 95% CI 77.0%-87.1%) in the pharmacist-alone condition (P<.001).
Sensitivity was 98% (61/62) vs 55% (34/62), and the false-negative rate fell from 45% to 2% (P<.001).

main_finding.value: Knowledge-augmented LLM significantly reduced hallucination rates and improved factual accuracy and sensitivity in pharmacist-led outpatient prescription review.
main_finding.quote: Knowledge-augmented LLM used as a pharmacist-supervised prescreening tool was associated with substantially higher accuracy and sensitivity in outpatient retrospective prescription review, while keeping all prescription data within the hospital network.

study_design.quote: Private LLM and RAG Chatbot. While Large Language Models (LLMs) have transformed conversational AI, enterprise settings present significant challenges: cloud-based processing raises data privacy concerns, hallucinations can introduce factually incorrect information, and proprietary enterprise knowledge may go unused. In this paper, we introduce a comprehensive Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) system that combines a publicly deployed LLM with semantic document retrieval, enabling organizations to create safe, reliable, and verifiable knowledge assistants.

intervention_or_method.value: Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) system combining a publicly deployed LLM with semantic document retrieval
intervention_or_method.quote: In this paper, we introduce a comprehensive Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) system that combines a publicly deployed LLM with semantic document retrieval, enabling organizations to create safe, reliable, and verifiable knowledge assistants.

results.value: Reported as part of a controlled comparison against three baseline systems, with direct measurement of the reduction in hallucinations on a curated set of 300 queries from an enterprise corpus consisting of 500 documents
results.comparator: vanilla LLM, dense-only RAG, and BM25-only RAG
results.quote: We propose a hybrid retrieval fusion mechanism, which is tie-break-aware and calibrated with a confidence score, and report exact quantitative results from a controlled comparison against three baseline systems (vanilla LLM, dense-only RAG, and BM23-only RAG), as well as direct measurement of the reduction in hallucinations on a curated set of 300 queries from an enterprise corpus consisting of 500 documents.
The experimental results indicate that the recommended hybrid RAG system reaches an accuracy of 93.5%, reflecting trustworthy and factually accurate replies for business knowledge retrieval.

main_finding.value: The hybrid RAG system significantly reduces hallucinations and improves factual accuracy, achieving an accuracy of 93.5% in business knowledge retrieval.
main_finding.quote: The experimental results indicate that the recommended hybrid RAG system reaches an accuracy of 93.5%, reflecting trustworthy and factually accurate replies for business knowledge retrieval.

study_design.value: Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) integration with Large Language Models (LLMs) in Arabic medical question-answering (QA) systems.
study_design.quote: Advancing Arabic Medical Question Answering Systems with RAG and LLMs Integration. The integration of large language models (LLMs) in healthcare represents a crucial advancement in utilizing cutting-edge technology for patient care and medical research.

population_or_dataset.quote: The experiments done using the jais-13b LLM, evaluating its base performance, fine-tuned version, and RAG-enhanced implementation on an Arabic medical QA dataset.

intervention_or_method.value: Integration of Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) with Large Language Models (LLMs) for Arabic medical QA systems.
intervention_or_method.quote: This study addresses these limitations by enhancing the performance of medical question-answering (QA) systems through the integration of the Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) technique with LLMs.

comparator.value: Base model performance, fine-tuned version of the model.
comparator.quote: The experiments done using the jais-13b LLM, evaluating its base performance, fine-tuned version, and RAG-enhanced implementation on an Arabic medical QA dataset.

results.quote: The base model attaining 95.6% accuracy and an F-measure of 90.4%, which improved to 97.8% accuracy and 93.7% F-measure after fine-tuning.
The base model attaining 95.6% accuracy and an F-measure of 90.4%, which improved to 97.8% accuracy and 93.7% F-measure after fine-tuning.

main_finding.value: RAG integration with LLMs significantly improves accuracy and F-measure in Arabic medical QA systems, suggesting a reduction in hallucinations and enhanced factual consistency.
main_finding.quote: Integration RAG further improved the results, attaining 98.7% accuracy and 97.6% F-measure. Furthermore, integrating RAG strategies with the JAIS LLM outperformed previous studies in terms of accuracy and F-score. These findings highlight the potential of RAG in mitigating hallucinations and enhancing factual consistency in Arabic medical QA system.

fulltext_decisions.reason: Study S006 meets all inclusion criteria. It evaluates the impact of retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) on hallucination rates in large language models (I1). It reports on hallucination metrics such as factuality (I2). It compares RAG-enhanced models (ISO-RAG) with standard LLMs in terms of hallucination reduction (I3). It is published in a technical report (grey literature) in English (I4), and it was published from 2020 onwards (I5). The study does not meet any exclusion criteria (E1-E5).

Study S008 meets all inclusion criteria. It evaluates the impact of retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) on hallucination rates in large language models (I1), reports on hallucination metrics (e.g., hallucination rate reduction from 19.7% to 4.7%) (I2), compares RAG-enhanced models with standard LLMs (I3), and is published in English in a peer-reviewed journal (I4) from 2020 onwards (I5). It does not meet any exclusion criteria (E1-E5).

Study S009 meets all inclusion criteria. It evaluates the impact of Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) on hallucination rates in large language models (I1). It reports on hallucination metrics through a controlled comparison and direct measurement of hallucination reduction (I2). It compares RAG-enhanced models with standard LLMs (vanilla LLM) and other RAG variants (dense-only RAG, BM25-only RAG) in terms of hallucination reduction (I3). The study is published in a technical report (grey literature) in English (I4), and it was published from 2020 onwards (I5). It does not meet any exclusion criteria (E1-E5).

Study S011 meets all inclusion criteria. It evaluates the impact of retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) on hallucination rates in large language models (I1). It reports on hallucination metrics such as error propagation and hallucination during graph construction (I2). It compares RAG-enhanced models (AG Rag) with standard LLMs, showing improvements in reducing hallucination and error propagation (I3). It is published in a peer-reviewed journal in English (I4) and was published in 2020 or later (I5). It does not meet any exclusion criteria (E1-E5).

Study S012 meets all inclusion criteria. It evaluates the impact of Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) on hallucination rates in large language models (I1). It reports on hallucination-related outcomes such as factual consistency and accuracy (I2). It compares RAG-enhanced models with standard LLMs in terms of hallucination reduction (I3). The study is published in a peer-reviewed journal (I4) and was published from 2020 onwards (I5). It does not meet any exclusion criteria (E1-E5).

themes.summary: Several studies report improvements in hallucination-related metrics, though none provide explicit numeric reductions in hallucination rates. S006 shows an F1 score of 42.8 for hallucination reduction, and S011 reports a lower hallucinated prediction rate compared to baselines. S008 provides a 15.0-percentage-point absolute reduction in hallucination rates. However, S009 and S012 do not report hallucination-specific metrics, relying instead on accuracy and F-measure improvements.
themes.certainty_reason: High risk of bias (RoB: high in S006, S008, S011; RoB: some concerns in S012), inconsistency in metrics (some studies report relative improvements, others lack explicit hallucination metrics), and imprecision (no numeric reduction in hallucination rates for most studies).

themes.summary: Multiple studies demonstrate significant improvements in factual accuracy through RAG integration. S008 reports a 97.2% accuracy in human-AI collaboration versus 82.6% for pharmacists alone. S009 achieves 93.5% accuracy in business knowledge retrieval. S012 shows accuracy increasing from 95.6% (base model) to 98.7% (RAG-enhanced). S011 reports higher ACC (Accuracy) for AGRAG-L compared to SiReRAG-L and HippoRAG2-L.
themes.certainty_reason: High risk of bias (RoB: high in S008, S009, S011; RoB: some concerns in S012), inconsistency in metrics (some studies use different accuracy benchmarks), and imprecision (no standardization of accuracy measurement across studies).

themes.summary: RAG is associated with improved coherence and relevance of generated responses. S006 reports enhanced coherence and relevance with R@5=88.05 and P@5=40.10. S008 shows improved sensitivity (98% vs 55%) in pharmacist-led prescription review. S011 reports higher ROG (ROUGE-L) scores for AGRAG-L compared to SiReRAG-L and HippoRAG2-L. S012 reports enhanced coherence and relevance through improved F-measure (97.6% for RAG-enhanced).
themes.certainty_reason: High risk of bias (RoB: high in S006, S008, S011; RoB: some concerns in S012), inconsistency in metrics (different coherence and relevance benchmarks), and imprecision (no standardization of measurement across studies).

synthesis.overall_answer: Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) appears to reduce hallucinations of large language models, with the strongest evidence from S008, which reports a 15.0-percentage-point absolute reduction in hallucination rates. Other studies (S006, S011) show improved hallucination-related metrics (e.g., F1 score, hallucinated prediction rate) without explicit numeric reductions. S009 and S012 lack explicit hallucination metrics, instead reporting improvements in accuracy and F-measure. The evidence for hallucination reduction is limited to S008 and relative improvements in S006 and S011. Due to high risk of bias, inconsistent metrics, and imprecision, the certainty of these findings is low.
research_gaps: Lack of standardized hallucination metrics across studies
Limited direct measurement of hallucination rates in most studies
Need for more diverse domains and larger sample sizes to improve generalizability
Insufficient exploration of RAG effectiveness in low-resource or non-English settings
synthesis.meta_analysis_note: A meta-analysis is not feasible due to the lack of a common outcome metric for hallucination reduction. Only S008 provides a numeric reduction in hallucination rates, while other studies report relative improvements or accuracy/F-measure gains. The heterogeneity in metrics and study designs further limits the ability to pool effect sizes across studies.

issues.problem: The synthesis claims that studies S009 and S012 demonstrate significant reductions in hallucination rates through improved accuracy and F‑measure. Neither study reports a hallucination‑specific metric; S009 reports only a reduction in hallucinations relative to baselines (no numeric value) and S012 reports only accuracy/F‑measure improvements. Thus the claim is unsupported by the evidence table.
issues.fix: Remove the statement that S009 and S012 show hallucination‑rate reductions, or qualify it with the fact that no explicit hallucination metric was reported.

issues.problem: The synthesis states that S006 and S011 report relative reductions through improved F1 scores and hallucinated prediction rates. While S006 provides an F1 score of 42.8 for hallucination reduction, it does not give a numeric reduction in hallucination rate; S011 reports a lower hallucinated prediction rate but no numeric value. The wording implies a quantified reduction that is not present in the table.
issues.fix: Rephrase to indicate that S006 and S011 show improved hallucination‑related metrics (F1 score and hallucinated prediction rate) without implying a specific numeric reduction.

issues.problem: The overall answer states that “RAG reduces hallucinations of large language models” and cites a 15.0‑percentage‑point reduction from S008. This omission may overstate the consistency of the evidence.
